# Æion Efficiency — turn any repository into a calm, self-checking machine for coding agents

> **For the agent reading this file:** you are about to change how a repository works.
> **Enter plan mode first.** Read this file, then the chapter you are asked to apply, then the
> repository. Propose a plan; change nothing until a human approves it.

This guide has seven phases, from the smallest particles to a galaxy. Each phase is useful on its
own, each builds on the one before, and none needs the others to be finished. Apply one at a time.

| Phase | Chapter | One line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Quarks (phase 1, below) | The rules everything is made of: a short `AGENTS.md`, policies, security, a tidy tree |
| 2 | Atoms (phase 2, below) | Code intelligence: native language servers, so the agent navigates instead of guessing |
| 3 | Molecules (phase 3, below) | Knowledge bound to code: docs, task state and links checked both ways; a tech-watch folder |
| 4 | Cells (phase 4, below) | Skills: the procedures you repeat, written once, loaded only when needed |
| 5 | Organisms (phase 5, below) | Hooks: reflexes that check every edit, refuse secrets, and sign off every task |
| 6 | Constellations (phase 6, below) | Loops: inner (the session), middle (branch, PR, review), outer (scheduled, read-only) |
| 7 | Galaxy (phase 7, below) | Memory and decisions: session retros, taste, a Decisions API; the system improves itself |

The goal is **small context, fast feedback and verifiable changes**. Automated checks reduce
routine review work; independent review and human decisions still matter. The seven habits have
a short name: CRAFTED (principles below).

## The four promises (read these before anything else)

1. **Harmless.** Nothing here overwrites what a repository already has. An existing `AGENTS.md`,
   `CLAUDE.md`, policy, hook, skill, CI job or convention **wins** over this guide. When they
   conflict, keep theirs and note the difference; when they overlap, merge into theirs.
2. **Plan first.** Every phase starts in plan mode: inspect, then propose the smallest change that
   fits the repository, then wait for a human's yes.
3. **Evidence, not claims.** A phase is done when its checks pass, not when files exist. Installed,
   configured, enabled and working are four different states; report each.
4. **No over-engineering.** Add a file, a tool or a rule only when it removes a real, repeated
   cost. Deleting a useless doc is progress.

## How to use it

- **An existing repository:** give your agent this file and one chapter at a time, in order:
  *"Read efficiency/00-EFFICIENCY.md and efficiency/1-quarks.md, then plan phase 1 for this repo."*
- **A new repository:** copy the whole Æion Factory as a starting point (its `README.md` says how)
  and walk the phases to adapt it.
- **Every phase ends the same way:** checks run, results reported, docs and task state updated,
  one pull request, one review comment.

## Assumptions

- Claude Code, local Codex, OpenCode and Pi share instructions, Knowledge and maintained skills.
  Native hooks/configuration differ; follow each setup in Æion Factory README and compatibility
  runbook. Claude plugins remain Claude-specific; token guarantees are not assumed portable.
- A git repository on a forge with pull requests (GitHub examples; others work the same way).
- Nothing in this guide needs a paid service beyond the agent itself; optional integrations
  (a Decisions API, a memory service) stay **off** until someone turns them on.

## Credits

The ideas here stand on other people's work; see the credits (at the end of this file). In particular the
skill anatomy follows Addy Osmani's `agent-skills` (MIT), and the hook, security and skill tooling
comes from Anthropic's official Claude Code plugins.

# CRAFTED — seven useful habits for coding agents

CRAFTED is Æion's mnemonic for the existing seven phases. It is a practical guide, not an
established external standard or a promise of autonomous correctness.

| | Principle | Phase | A concrete starting point |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C | **Clarify the context.** | Quarks (phase 1, below) | A short AGENTS.md with purpose, boundaries and verification commands. |
| R | **Read the actual code.** | Atoms (phase 2, below) | Follow a definition, inspect callers, then verify project diagnostics. |
| A | **Anchor docs to code.** | Molecules (phase 3, below) | A source pointer that tools/knowledge/doc-links can resolve. |
| F | **Follow proven procedures.** | Cells (phase 4, below) | One focused skill for a task that actually repeats. |
| T | **Turn checks into reflexes.** | Organisms (phase 5, below) | A hook near the edit and the same relevant check in CI. |
| E | **Examine every change.** | Constellations (phase 6, below) | A branch, a real diff, independent review and current CI evidence. |
| D | **Document the evidence.** | Galaxy (phase 7, below) | A sourced decision or a verified lesson for the next session. |

## Try the core checks

Run these from an Æion Factory checkout with Python 3 available:

~~~sh
tools/knowledge/knowledge-check
tools/knowledge/doc-links
tools/repo-health/repo-health
~~~

They check document structure, links and repository size limits. They do not prove every written
claim or replace the application's tests, review and production safeguards.

For an existing repository, its instructions win. Apply one chapter at a time, with an approved
plan and a reviewable change. Optional loops, external memory and APIs are not prerequisites.

# Phase 1 — Quarks: the rules everything is made of

> *Before atoms, there are quarks. Before a smart agent, there are three short files it reads first.*

**In one line:** a short `AGENTS.md` that routes, a few durable policies, a security baseline, and
a tree an agent can understand in one look.

> **Agent:** enter plan mode. Inventory what the repository already has (step 1) before proposing
> anything. Existing instructions win; you merge into them, never replace them.

## Why

- Instruction files help an agent most when they are short and specific: an `AGENTS.md` is
  associated with about 28 % lower median runtime and 17 % fewer output tokens (Lulla et al.,
  2026), while generic repository overviews add cost without improving success (Gloaguen et al.,
  2026). Long context degrades every model measured (Chroma, *Context Rot*, 2025).
- So: route, don't explain. Point at the doc; let the agent open it when the task needs it.

## What the agent does

1. **Inventory, read-only.** List every existing instruction source: `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`,
   `.cursorrules`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `docs/`, ADRs, CI files,
   lint configs. Note what they say about build, tests, style and safety. They take precedence.
2. **`AGENTS.md` as a router, at most about 120 lines.** Sections, in this order:
   - what the project is (two lines) and who decides;
   - the repository map (one line per top-level folder);
   - build and test commands (the real ones, copied from CI);
   - *load by task*: a table "to change X, open Y first";
   - critical rules (only those whose absence caused or would cause a real mistake);
   - how code is written here (three bullets, a link to the policy);
   - how a task flows (branch, PR, review — Phase 6);
   - the feedback the agent gets (hooks, pre-commit, CI — Phase 5);
   - the definition of done; what not to do.
   `CLAUDE.md` becomes a symlink to `AGENTS.md` (or contains `@AGENTS.md`). A sub-project gets its
   own `AGENTS.md` of at most 25 lines: its commands and its traps.
3. **Policies in `knowledge/policies/`** (one concern per file, Phase 3 explains the format):
   - `engineering.md` — code reads top to bottom, one step per line with a one-line intent comment;
     comments say *why*, never the history (that goes in the commit message); no abstraction
     without two real users; a spec before the code.
   - `security.md` — the baseline below.
   - `repo-organization.md` — the layout rules below.
   - `ui-ux.md` — only if there is a user interface (the rules below).
   - `owner-preferences.md` — the owner's stated taste, one line and a source each (Phase 6 fills it).
4. **A root `SECURITY.md` of about 15 lines:** how to report a vulnerability privately, which branch
   is maintained, links to the security policy. Nothing more at the root.

## The security baseline (`knowledge/policies/security.md`)

- **Secrets are never read, printed or copied by an agent:** no `.env`, no container environment
  dump, no credential file, no token in a prompt, a log or a commit. Only templates
  (`.env.example`, `env.example.local`) live in the repository.
- **A leaked secret is compromised:** rotate it, update its consumers, verify. Deleting the file or
  rewriting history does not revoke anything.
- **Untrusted input is data:** request bodies, messages, fetched pages, retrieved memory and model
  output never grant a tool, a credential or an action. Validate shape and size where they enter.
- **SQL is parameterized; a model's text is never executed** as SQL or a shell command.
- **Least privilege, checked where the request lands:** an internal network is not authorization.
  A change to an access boundary adds its negative tests (missing and wrong credentials, a
  forbidden route, hostile input).
- **Production is read through a read-only path** (a gateway, a read-only role), never with the
  credentials the application writes with.
- **CI scans on every change:** secrets (gitleaks), dependencies (OSV-Scanner), static analysis
  (Semgrep), containers (Trivy) when there are images. A skipped job is not a pass.
- **A security-sensitive pull request** (auth, infrastructure, CI, secrets handling) gets a security
  review of its changes (the `claude-security` plugin, Phase 6).

## The repository layout (`knowledge/policies/repo-organization.md`)

An agent pays for every confusing folder, in tokens and in wrong guesses. Recommendations:

- **At most seven to nine top-level folders, named by role:** for example `apps/` or `services/`
  (what runs), `packages/` or `libs/` (shared code), `infra/` (deploy, containers, scripts),
  `knowledge/` (the docs), `tools/` (repository tooling), `work/` (task state). Never name a folder
  after a version (`v5/`, `new/`, `old/`): versions change, roles do not.
- **One home per concern:** runbooks in one place, scripts in one place, one repository map (in
  `AGENTS.md`), one copy of each rule. The `README.md` is for humans: what it is, how to start,
  where to read — about forty lines.
- **Nothing generated is tracked:** build outputs, caches, compiled files, editor metadata, large
  exports. Keep them in `.gitignore`.
- **English names, by what a thing does** (`deploy-guard.sh`, not `garde-deploiement.sh`).
- **A move is one pull request** that updates every reference (grep the old path: build files,
  container contexts, CI, deploy scripts, docs, hooks, skills, absolute paths on servers). If a path
  is used at runtime, the move ships with a deploy.
- **Delete before you add:** stale reports, duplicated maps, dead pointers to removed docs.

## The UI/UX rules (`knowledge/policies/ui-ux.md`, only with a UI)

Sober and exact rather than decorative:

- Every colour, radius, font and spacing value is a token in **one** file, with a light and a dark
  set; a hard-coded colour is a dark-mode bug. Text meets WCAG AA contrast (4.5:1).
- One primary colour and one accent; amber and red only for meaning (warning, danger).
- Phone first: check every changed screen at 375 px and 1440 px, light and dark. Tables become
  stacked cards on small screens; touch targets are at least 44 px.
- A plain wordmark; no decoration that carries no information; motion only to show a change of
  state, and none under reduced motion.
- An unknown or missing value reads "unknown", never "fine". A blank is not zero.
- Shared building blocks (page header, section, stat, meter, list, card) before any new component.
- A visual change gets a human's visual yes before it ships.

## Files this phase creates or merges into

| File | Note |
| --- | --- |
| `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` (symlink) | merge into the existing one if present |
| `knowledge/policies/{engineering,security,repo-organization,ui-ux,owner-preferences}.md` | skip a concern an existing doc already covers; link to it instead |
| `SECURITY.md` | only if absent |
| `.gitignore` entries | additions only |

## Done when

- `AGENTS.md` (and each nested one) is within its cap, and every command it names runs.
- Every rule in it has a reason a reviewer would accept; nothing in it repeats a doc.
- The CI scans exist (or the plan records why not).
- The layout plan is written as a list of moves with their references, even if not applied yet.

## Pitfalls

- Writing a long, friendly overview "for context": it costs tokens on every task and helps none.
- Copying a rule into several files: they drift. One home, links elsewhere.
- Renaming folders without a grep of every reference, including the ones on servers.

# Phase 2 — Atoms: code intelligence with native language servers

> *An atom knows its neighbours. An agent with a language server knows where a symbol is defined,
> who calls it, and that the line it just wrote does not compile — before the tests say so.*

**In one line:** register each language's own server with Claude Code, prove it navigates and
reports diagnostics, and keep its data out of the repository.

> **Agent:** enter plan mode. List the languages, their project-local tool versions, and any
> language-server setup that already exists. Reuse a working one; never install a second
> toolchain to match a guide.

## Why

Without a server the agent greps and guesses; with one it gets definitions, references, call
hierarchy and **diagnostics pushed into its context after each edit**, for a few tokens. Claude
Code exposes this as the `LSP` tool plus automatic diagnostics.

## The rules that make it work

1. **One server per file extension.** Claude Code gives each extension to the first enabled
   server; a second one is silently unused. Two servers for `.ts` (Node and Deno, say) means one
   session per scope, not both at once.
2. **The project's own binary, never a global one.** The server must match the compiler the
   build uses: resolve it from the project (`node_modules/.bin`, the repository's JDK).
3. **Native servers first:**

   | Language | Server | Start |
   | --- | --- | --- |
   | TypeScript 7+ | the native compiler | `node_modules/.bin/tsc --lsp --stdio` (TypeScript 7 ships no tsserver; older wrappers do not fit) |
   | TypeScript ≤ 6 | `typescript-language-server` | `typescript-language-server --stdio` |
   | Deno | built in | `deno lsp` |
   | Java | Eclipse JDT LS (Java 21+ to run; compiles 8–25) | its `bin/jdtls` launcher with `--java-executable <the project JDK>` and `-data <a folder outside the repo>` |
   | Python | Pyright | `pyright-langserver --stdio` |
   | Go | gopls | `gopls serve` |
   | Rust | rust-analyzer | `rust-analyzer` |

4. **Server data lives outside the repository.** JDT LS writes Eclipse files (`.project`,
   `.classpath`, `.settings/`) into every module unless the JVM gets
   `-Djava.import.generatesMetadataFilesAtProjectRoot=false` (its launcher's `--jvm-arg=`); the
   initialization option of the same name alone did not stop it with JDT LS 1.63. Put its workspace
   under the user's cache folder, and check `git status` after the first import.
5. **Stdout is the protocol.** A launcher prints nothing on stdout; messages go to stderr.

## How to register them

The smallest supported way is a **local plugin** that contains only the registration:

```
tools/claude-plugins/
  .claude-plugin/marketplace.json      # lists the plugins below
  native-lsp/
    .claude-plugin/plugin.json
    .lsp.json                          # server name -> command, args, extensionToLanguage
    scripts/<launchers>                # resolve the project's binary, then exec it
```

- In `.lsp.json`, `command` and `args` may use `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` and `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}`.
  Every field is strict: an unknown key makes the whole file be skipped.
- Add the marketplace and install the plugin at project scope:
  `claude plugin marketplace add ./tools/claude-plugins --scope project` then
  `claude plugin install native-lsp@<marketplace> --scope project`. A marketplace added from a
  local path loads in place, so the launchers stay in the repository.
- `claude plugin validate <dir>` checks the manifest; it does **not** read `.lsp.json`. Look in
  `/plugin` → Errors for `Invalid LSP server config` or `Executable not found`.

The Æion Factory ships this plugin (`tools/claude-plugins/native-lsp`) with launchers for
TypeScript 7, Deno and Java; copy only the servers you need.

## Proving it (each is a separate state: installed, registered, enabled, loaded, working)

1. **Handshake:** the launcher answers an LSP `initialize` with its server name and version.
2. **Navigation, inside Claude Code:** ask the agent to find the definition and the references of
   a real symbol through the `LSP` tool.
3. **Diagnostics:** in a throwaway file, write a deliberate type error; Claude Code must report it
   after the edit, then stop reporting it once fixed. Delete the file.
4. **Persistence:** start a fresh session; the server is still enabled and answers.

If navigation works and diagnostics do not, the result is *partial*: say so.

## Files this phase creates or merges into

| File | Note |
| --- | --- |
| `tools/claude-plugins/**` | only the servers this repository uses |
| `.claude/settings.json` (project scope) | `enabledPlugins` and the local marketplace; written by the CLI |
| `knowledge/operations/build-and-test.md` | a short "Language servers" section: servers, versions, how to switch scopes, how to roll back |

## Done when

Every language in the repository has a working server (or a written reason why not), the four
proofs above passed per server, and no tool data appeared in `git status`.

## Pitfalls

- A registration that points at a global `tsc` or a second JDK: diagnostics then disagree with CI.
- Enabling two servers for the same extension and assuming directory-aware routing.
- Leaving generated IDE files in the tree after a first JDT LS run.

# Phase 3 — Molecules: knowledge bound to code

> *Atoms bind into molecules. Docs bind to the code they describe — and a check notices when one
> moves without the other.*

**In one line:** one canonical knowledge base, one task-state file, docs and code linked both
ways and checked, and a technical-watch folder that keeps the repository's ideas fresh.

> **Agent:** enter plan mode. Map the docs that exist (README, `docs/`, wiki exports, ADRs). Move
> facts into the structure below only where it removes a duplicate or a stale copy; link the rest.

## Why

Docs drift because nothing tells anyone they are wrong. A link costs nothing until it is followed
(Anthropic, *Effective context engineering*: keep lightweight identifiers, load content just in
time), and a deterministic check turns "the doc is probably stale" into a failing line. Research on
doc-to-code trace links finds that naming-based guesses produce most false links; explicit links
remove the guess.

## The structure

```
knowledge/
  index.md            # one table: "to do X, open Y"
  architecture/       # how the parts fit; flows; invariants across components
  components/         # one doc per unit, in the spec format below
  decisions/          # ADRs: context, decision, consequences; superseded, never edited away
  policies/           # durable rules (Phase 1)
  operations/         # build and test, deploy, runbooks, recovery
  references/         # external material still worth keeping (summaries, links)
  current/            # volatile state summaries, each with a stale_after date
work/current.md       # task state only — never knowledge
tech-watch/           # the technical watch (below)
```

**Each concept has a small frontmatter:** `type`, `title`, `description` (at most 250
characters), `status` (draft | stable | deprecated), `generated` (`by`, `at`), `sources` (what the
doc is built from, including the **code files it describes**), and at most three `verified`
entries of at most 300 characters (what was checked, the result, the command or commit). The body
stays under about 600 lines; a longer doc splits along its headings.

**A component doc is a spec**, written before the code changes: *Intent; Data sources; Inputs;
Outputs (every refusal and error); Invariants (each names its test); Determinism (deterministic,
bounded or adaptive, and why); Acceptance checks (commands that pass or fail); Out of scope.*

**`work/current.md`** holds open tasks only, newest first, at most 150 lines, each entry at most 10
lines with five fields: *Owner decision; State; Next (who); Blocker; Evidence.* A finished task is
deleted — the commit message and the knowledge base keep what matters.

## Links both ways, and the check

- **Doc to code:** the doc's `sources` lists the files it describes
  (`resource: ../../src/billing/invoice.ts`). A directory source is checked for existence only.
- **Code to doc:** a file a doc describes carries one header line `Spec: knowledge/<doc>.md`.
- Explicit file paths work independently of language or extension, including spaces and Unicode.
  Header discovery scans the first 8 KiB of leading comments/docstrings in tracked regular text
  files; Markdown, vendored/dependency/cache content, known secrets and symlinks are excluded.
  For formats without comments, use `sources`. This does not install language tools or validate syntax.
- **`tools/knowledge/doc-links`** (shipped with Æion Factory, Python standard library only):
  - **L1** a `Spec:` pointer resolves; **L2** every `sources` path exists;
  - **L3** with `--diff <base>` (`origin/develop`, else `origin/main`): a file changed while a doc covering it did not. Updating the
    doc passes, and so does a commit trailer
    `Docs-Checked: knowledge/<doc>.md -- <why no documented fact changed>`. A diff that only adds or
    removes `Spec:` lines moves no fact and passes.
- Run L1/L2 in the pre-commit, L3 in CI on pull requests, and let the hooks of Phase 5 remind the
  agent at edit time and before it stops.
- **Performance:** a link is a path, not content, so it adds nothing to context until followed; the
  check reads the tree in about a second for a repository of a thousand files.

## The technical watch — this phase creates `tech-watch/`

Create a `tech-watch/` folder in English with:

- `tech-watch/README.md` — the method (copy Æion Factory's): start from current evidence (read
  `AGENTS.md`, the knowledge index, `work/current.md`; record the commit and a cutoff date), form
  findings before reading older reports, search primary sources (official docs, release and
  security notes for the **versions the project actually pins**, papers, credible practitioners),
  open the original behind every post, record date and method, and give each idea one decision:
  *adopt, evaluate, retain, defer or reject*, with its local fit and smallest useful experiment.
  "Nothing worth changing" is a valid result. No new dependency or platform without a shown need.
- `tech-watch/pending/index.md` — how to find pending packages: each watch writes one dated folder
  `tech-watch/pending/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>/index.md` with a table (ID, priority, state, smallest next
  action, acceptance). Items close as *implemented, already fixed, not applicable, declined* or
  *tracked elsewhere* (with a real destination); when all are closed, the folder is deleted — git is
  the archive.

The outer loop (Phase 6) runs the watch on a schedule.

## Files this phase creates or merges into

`knowledge/**` (index and folder indexes first), `work/current.md`, `tech-watch/README.md`,
`tech-watch/pending/index.md`, `tools/knowledge/{knowledge-check,doc-links}` and their tests.

## Done when

`knowledge-check` and `doc-links` pass; every component that changed recently has a spec; the
README no longer repeats the map or the rules; `work/current.md` holds only open tasks.

## Pitfalls

- A knowledge base that is a journal: dated narratives belong in commit messages.
- `verified` lists that grow forever: three entries, the newest.
- Linking whole directories and expecting the diff check to bite: only exact files count.

# Phase 4 — Cells: skills, the procedures you repeat

> *A cell is a molecule that does one job, again and again, without being told twice.*

**In one line:** every procedure the team repeats becomes a short skill with a verification gate,
loaded only when it is needed.

> **Agent:** enter plan mode. List the procedures this repository repeats (deploy, release, review,
> migration, a data fix) and the corrections a human has had to make twice. Those are the skills.

## Why

A skill costs only its name and one-line description until it is used; its body loads on demand.
That makes it the cheapest place for a long procedure — far cheaper than `AGENTS.md`, which is read
on every task. And a written procedure with a gate does not forget the gate at 2 a.m.

## Anatomy of a good skill

Following Addy Osmani's `agent-skills` anatomy (MIT), adapted:

```markdown
---
name: kebab-case-name            # matches the folder
description: What it does, in the third person. Use when <the trigger>.   # <= ~1000 chars
---

# Title

## Overview        — what and why, three lines, a link to the policy that gives the reasons
## When to use     — triggers, and when NOT to use it
## Process         — numbered steps, each with the exact command
## Rationalizations — | Excuse | Rebuttal |  (the shortcuts an agent will be tempted by)
## Red flags       — signs the procedure is going wrong
## Verification    — checklist items that each need evidence
```

- **Short:** aim for under 60 lines; never over 500. Long material moves to a file beside it
  (`references/`, `scripts/`), one level deep.
- **Never copy a rule** into a skill: link the policy. A skill is *how*, a policy is *why*.
- **Dangerous skills are manual:** `disable-model-invocation: true` (deploy, a data migration).
- **Path-scoped instructions** that should load only near some files go in `.claude/rules/<area>.md`
  with a `paths:` glob list, not in a skill.

## The lifecycle set shipped with Æion Factory

| Skill | Use when |
| --- | --- |
| `plan` | starting any non-trivial task: inspect, propose, wait for a yes |
| `spec` | a feature or component changes: write the spec sections first |
| `build` | implementing in thin, tested slices |
| `test` | adding or fixing tests; the test pyramid; never weaken an assertion |
| `sign-off` | ending a task: tests, docs and links, task state, security on sensitive diffs |
| `pr-review` | a pull request is open: fresh reviewer, verified findings, one verdict comment |
| `ship` | merging and releasing: green CI, changelog, the deploy's own guards |
| `okf-update` | a documented fact changed: the right doc, its links, its caps |
| `security-scan` | a sensitive diff, or the weekly outer loop: `claude-security` |
| `tech-watch` | the monthly watch (Phase 3's method) |
| `pr-taste` | the owner commented on a PR: durable preferences into the knowledge base |
| `retro` | after a session or weekly: lessons, new hook rules, new skills (Phase 7) |
| `graph` | before changing or tracing code: exact structural answers from `tools/architecture/ask` |
| `loop-triage` | an outer-loop finding: turn it into an issue an inner loop can pick up |
| `adopt` | applying this guide to an existing repository, phase by phase |

## Creating and testing skills: `skill-creator`

Anthropic's `skill-creator` plugin (`/plugin install skill-creator@claude-plugins-official`):

1. Interviews you for the intent, edge cases and success criteria, then drafts the `SKILL.md`.
2. Writes 2–3 realistic prompts to `evals/evals.json`, runs them **with and without** the skill in
   parallel subagents, grades each run, and aggregates a benchmark you review.
3. Optimizes the `description` against ~20 trigger and near-miss queries, so the skill loads when
   it should and only then.

Rule of thumb: **a correction made twice becomes a skill or a hook** (a hook if a regex can check
it — Phase 5; a skill if it needs judgement).

## Done when

Each repeated procedure has a skill under its cap; dangerous ones are manual-only; each skill has
been run once for real (or evaluated with `skill-creator`) and its verification items checked.

## Pitfalls

- A skill that restates `AGENTS.md`: delete it.
- A vague description ("helps with deploys"): it will load at the wrong time or never.
- Skills without a verification section: the agent will declare success on vibes.

# Phase 5 — Organisms: hooks, the reflexes

> *An organism does not decide to pull its hand from the fire. A good repository does not wait for
> review to notice a secret, a broken link or a stale doc.*

**In one line:** fast, silent-on-success hooks that check every edit, refuse dangerous commands,
and sign off a task before the agent stops — written **after** the docs, to enforce rules that
already exist.

> **Agent:** enter plan mode. List existing hooks (`.claude/settings.json`, git hooks, CI). Propose
> only hooks that enforce a rule written in Phases 1–3. Docs first, hooks second: a hook never
> invents a rule.

## Why

Instructions are context; hooks are enforcement (Claude Code docs: to block an action, use a
hook). Feedback within three seconds of a mistake is the cheapest correction there is — it costs a
few lines of context instead of a failed CI run and a second pull request.

## The reflexes

| Reflex | Event | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Orientation** | `SessionStart` (startup, resume, compact) | prints at most 25 lines: `git status`, the last commits, the open tasks of `work/current.md`, the health scorecard |
| **Guard** | `PreToolUse` on `Bash` and on `Read/Edit/Write/Grep` | refuses reading secret files, environment dumps, force-pushes and `--no-verify` (exit 2 with the reason) |
| **Check after edit** | `PostToolUse` on `Edit/Write` | runs only the checks that apply to the edited file (knowledge checks and documentation hints; add project lint/size checks explicitly); silent when fine, at most 15 lines when not; names the doc that covers the file, once |
| **Sign-off** | `Stop` | if the branch changed code without its covering docs, the task state or the map, blocks **once** with the list; the same findings never block twice, and a second stop always passes |
| **Pre-commit** | git `pre-commit` (`git config core.hooksPath tools/git-hooks`) | the same checks for every committer, human or agent |
| **Context checkpoint** | session, prompt, tool, compact and stop events | 250k alert and closure-only work; current handover/docs required before compaction; entire-run stop at observed 300k or unavailable usage |

Rules for every hook: under three seconds; exit 0 and silent on success; exit 2 with the rule and
its fix on failure; never a hook that loops (the sign-off uses `stop_hook_active` and a
per-session memory of what it already said); tested (`.claude/hooks/test_hooks.py`).
The context adapter has a five-second hook deadline and separate tests
(`tools/context/tests/test_budget.py`). Its strict pre-request ceiling is unqualified; see
`knowledge/operations/context-safety.md`. Claude, Codex, OpenCode and Pi share one context rule: a 250k closure alert, a verified handover, then compaction at 250k; 300k forces the handover and compaction again.
The adapters share guards/checkpoints, with the exact supported events and limits documented in
`knowledge/operations/agent-compatibility.md`; they do not copy Claude settings blindly.

## Rules from corrections: `hookify`

Anthropic's `hookify` plugin (`/plugin install hookify@claude-plugins-official`) writes simple
hook rules as Markdown files, `.claude/hookify.<name>.local.md`:

```markdown
---
name: warn-console-log
enabled: true
event: file              # bash | file | stop | prompt | all
conditions:
  - field: new_text
    operator: regex_match
    pattern: console\.log\(
action: warn             # or block
---
Remove debug logging before committing; use the project's logger.
```

- `/hookify <instruction>` writes a rule; `/hookify` alone reads the recent conversation and
  proposes rules from the corrections you made. Rules apply on the next tool use, no restart.
- Use it for **checkable taste** (a forbidden pattern, a required header) that the retro of Phase 7
  surfaces; keep logic-heavy checks in real scripts with tests.

## Files this phase creates or merges into

`.claude/settings.json` (hooks), `.claude/hooks/*.py` and their tests, `tools/git-hooks/pre-commit`,
`.claude/hookify.*.local.md` (examples, disabled until wanted), `.claude/rules/*.md` (path-scoped).

## Done when

A deliberate violation of each rule is caught in under three seconds (a secret read refused, a
broken link reported, a code change without its doc signed off once), and the hook tests pass in CI.

## Pitfalls

- A `Stop` hook that blocks every turn: an infinite, expensive loop. Block once per finding set.
- Hooks that print on success: context noise on every edit.
- A hook that silently auto-fixes: the agent learns nothing and the diff surprises the reviewer.

---

# Phase 6 — Constellations: inner, middle and outer loops

> *Organisms form constellations: patterns that repeat on their own schedule, each one small,
> together a system.*

**In one line:** three loops — the session (inner), the branch and pull request (middle), the
scheduled read-only checks (outer) — connected by issues, so problems found at night are fixed
by morning through the same reviewed path as any other change.

> **Agent:** enter plan mode. Find what already runs on a schedule (CI crons, monitors, scripts)
> and what reads production. The outer loop only ever **reads**; propose its read-only path first.

## The three loops

| Loop | Runs | Speed | What it guarantees |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Inner** | inside a session | seconds | plan → small steps → language-server diagnostics and hooks after each edit → tests → `sign-off` |
| **Middle** | per task | minutes | one branch per task → pull request → `pr-review` (fresh reviewer, one verdict comment) → green CI → merge |
| **Outer** | on a schedule | hours | read-only checks of production, security and docs → findings become issues → an inner loop picks them up |

(The inner/outer vocabulary comes from developer-experience practice: the inner loop is the fast
local edit-build-test cycle, the outer loop the integration, review and release around it.)

### Inner loop

- Plan mode for anything non-trivial (skill `plan`); thin slices (skill `build`); the reflexes of
  Phase 5 on every edit; tests before the claim (skill `test`).
- **Security inside the loop:** a diff that touches authentication, infrastructure, CI or secret
  handling gets `/claude-security` on its changes before the pull request (the `claude-security`
  plugin maps the code, searches it and has separate verifiers try to disprove each finding; only
  survivors are reported). Not on every diff — it costs tokens.
- Ends with the skill `sign-off`.

### Middle loop

- **One branch per task** (`task/<slug>`), small commits, `gh pr create` with what, why and the
  checks run.
- **`pr-review`:** a *fresh* subagent reviews the diff (fresh context catches what the author's
  context hides); every finding is verified before it is reported; one comment goes on the pull
  request:

  ```
  Review: OK            (or)   Review: NOT OK
  - <high|medium|low> path:line -- the finding (at most five)
  Checks: CI <state>; doc-links <result>; tests <what ran>
  ```

- **Merge after `Review: OK` and a green CI**: a task pull request may squash; a release pull request
  (`develop → main`) is merged with a merge commit, never squashed. A change that needs a deploy or a human
  decision (money, risk, data deletion, a policy) waits for that human.
- **Taste:** the skill `pr-taste` reads the owner's pull-request comments and keeps the durable
  ones — architecture, naming, style, security, UI — in `knowledge/policies/owner-preferences.md`,
  one line and a source each; a checkable one becomes a `hookify` rule. The next review applies
  them, so the owner never has to say it twice.
- The same comment becomes the input of the next review: corrections compound.
- Every main update runs the mandatory Graphify/Archify round, including docs-only merges.
  Keep the complete architecture spec current and wait for the exact merged SHA's passing
  analysis before closing work or releasing (`knowledge/operations/architecture-maintenance.md`).

### Outer loop (scheduled, read-only)

A scheduler — **mandatory**, whichever kind you have — runs `loops/orchestrator.sh <job>` headless
(`claude -p`), each job with its own prompt, model, tool allowlist and budget:
The orchestrator uses `tools/context/run`; the project needs a verified initial architecture
baseline and inherits the same context checkpoints as interactive managed runs.

| Job | Default schedule | Reads | Writes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `outer` health | daily | production through the read-only path (a gateway, a read-only role), CI history | issues |
| `security` | weekly, and before each release | the codebase (`claude-security` scan at medium effort) | issues, a report folder (git-ignored) |
| `docs` | daily | `doc-links`, `knowledge-check`, stale `stale_after` dates | issues |
| `watch` | monthly | the tech-watch method (Phase 3) | a `tech-watch/pending/<date>-<topic>/` package via PR |
| `retro` | weekly | the week's sessions and PR comments (Phase 7) | a PR with lessons, hook rules, skills (`skill-creator`, `hookify`) |

- **Findings become issues**, not fixes: `gh issue create` with labels `loop:outer`,
  `severity:<high|medium|low>`, and `agent-ready` when the fix is clear and small, `needs-owner`
  otherwise (see `loops/issue-protocol.md`).
- **An inner loop picks up `agent-ready` issues** (`loops/orchestrator.sh inner --issue <n>`): one
  issue, one branch, one pull request, the normal middle loop. Nothing reaches the default branch
  without a review comment and a green CI.
- **Safety by construction:** the outer jobs run with a read-only tool allowlist, no secrets in
  their context, a default 30-turn / 900-second budget, and a kill switch (`LOOPS_ENABLED=false`). They never deploy,
  restart, migrate data or change a setting.

### Model routing: `auto`

Every loop defaults to model and thinking level `auto` when no local override exists. The orchestrator
picks by the job's criticality: a small, fast model (e.g. Haiku) for triage and read-only checks;
a balanced one (e.g. Sonnet) for implementation and reviews; the most capable (e.g. Opus) at high
effort for security, architecture and anything labelled `severity:high`. Pin a value to override.

### Schedulers

Pick the one you have; the jobs are the same:

- **GitHub Actions** (`.github/workflows/outer-loop.yml`, off until `OUTER_LOOP_ENABLED` is set):
  `on: schedule`, `anthropics/claude-code-action` with a prompt, or the orchestrator in a runner.
- **A machine that is always on:** `cron` or macOS `launchd` (`loops/schedules/`).
- **Claude's own scheduled tasks or routines**, where available.
- **Per release:** run `security` and `docs` as a release gate.

## Done when

The three loops ran once each for real: a task went branch → PR → review comment → merge; an
outer job opened an issue; an inner run fixed an `agent-ready` issue through a reviewed PR.

## Pitfalls

- An outer loop with write access "just for small fixes": every fix goes through the middle loop.
- Reviews by the author's own context: always a fresh reviewer.
- Scheduling everything daily: the security scan and the watch cost real tokens — weekly and
  monthly are enough.

---

# Phase 7 — Galaxy: memory, decisions, and a system that improves itself

> *Constellations drift into a galaxy: billions of small rules, one shape. The shape here is a
> repository that remembers what it learned, records why it decided, and gets cheaper every week.*

**In one line:** retrospectives turn sessions and reviews into rules, hooks and skills; an
optional Decisions API records and serves decisions; an optional memory service recalls what
mattered — and three numbers tell you whether any of it works.

> **Agent:** enter plan mode. Everything in this phase is optional and **off by default**. Propose
> turning on one piece at a time, with its cost and its privacy impact.

## Hindsight: learning from the sessions

Every coding session leaves a transcript (Claude Code keeps them locally, under
`~/.claude/projects/<project>/`). The skill `retro` reads the week's sessions and pull-request
comments and extracts four kinds of lesson:

| Lesson | Becomes |
| --- | --- |
| an error the agent repeated (a wrong command, a missed check) | a hook rule (`hookify`) or a line in a skill's red flags |
| a correction a human made twice | a hook if a regex can see it, otherwise a skill step |
| a stated preference (naming, style, UI, architecture) | a line in `owner-preferences.md` with its source |
| a procedure redone by hand | a new skill, drafted and evaluated with `skill-creator` |

It opens one pull request with the lessons; the middle loop reviews it like any other change.

**A memory service, if you want recall across sessions:** for example Hindsight
(`vectorize-io/hindsight`, MIT), which *retains* facts and experiences from conversations,
*recalls* them by combined vector, keyword, graph and time search, and *reflects* to form mental
models. It installs as Claude Code hooks (recall on each prompt, retain at the end). It stores
tool calls by default — keep it off for repositories with sensitive data, and never point it at
secrets. Keep the integration disabled until its data boundaries and benefit have been reviewed.

## A Decisions API: decisions as data

Some decisions should not live in a chat: "may agents upgrade this dependency?", "is this
threshold approved?", "who owns this area?". A Decisions API is an external service of record for
them — human or agent decisions with their reasons — that loops can read before acting.

- **The contract** (`loops/decisions-api/README.md`): `GET /decisions?topic=...` returns the
  current decision and its reason; `POST /decisions` records a proposed one for a human to approve.
  Every call carries `Authorization: Bearer $DECISION_API_SECRET`.
- **JEV is the example** in Æion Factory: an external decision service your loops can consult. Any
  service with that contract fits.
- **Off by default** (`DECISION_API_ENABLED=false`): the client refuses to run until it is turned
  on, and the secret lives only in the local env file, never in the repository or a prompt.
- **Authority stays explicit:** an agent may *read* a decision and *propose* one; only a human
  approves. A missing or unreachable decision means *no* — fail closed.

## The trinity, measured

The sweet spot is a balance, so measure it — weekly, in the retro:

| Measure | Why |
| --- | --- |
| tokens (or cost) per merged pull request | the price of a unit of work |
| time from branch to green merge | speed |
| share of pull requests merged with no human edit, and share of review findings that were real | how much review a human still has to do |

When cost rises, look for context bloat (a long `AGENTS.md`, skills loading too often). When time
rises, look for slow checks. When human edits rise, the retro has lessons to capture.

## How the galaxy turns

```
session  ──► hooks catch it now ──► sign-off ──► PR ──► review comment ──► merge
   ▲                                                         │
   │                                                         ▼
 skills / hooks / preferences  ◄── weekly retro ◄── sessions + PR comments + outer-loop issues
```

Each week the same mistake becomes a little rarer, because it now has a hook, a skill step or a
preference that the next review applies. That is the whole trick.

## Done when

One retro ran and its pull request merged; the trinity has a first measurement; any optional
service that was turned on has its cost, its data scope and its off switch written down.

## Pitfalls

- A memory service that recalls everything: noise is context rot with extra steps.
- A Decisions API that agents can approve themselves: it is no longer a record of decisions.
- Measuring only cost: the cheapest PR is the one nobody can trust.

  data-flow-oriented security inspection. Plugin-specific terms still apply; proprietary
  `claude-security` definitions are not transplanted into the cross-host pool.

  specialist workflow references. https://github.com/anthropics/knowledge-work-plugins

The versioned skills/catalog.json records exact source commits, entrypoint fingerprints and license
files. Native Factory text is selectively adapted, not a wholesale copy of upstream prompts. The separate passive pool contains upstream skill/agent files and supporting resources,
with three source-hash-bound scanner annotation comments recorded in tools/skills/annotations.json, with license texts under skills/licenses/.
No upstream agent-launch mandate, model setting or generic threshold is adopted.
